hero.standfirst: She grew up on a coffee farm in Karnataka and did not see snow until she was twenty. At thirty she took a World Cup start at 66°N in northern Finland.

standfirstSource.note: AP reports the coffee farm upbringing and that she did not see snow until age 20. Paraphrased, not quoted.

burst.note: Plays once on load, then settles on hero.image. Replace with video when footage exists.

hero.profileHeading: It started with a film, and a race on television.
hero.profileBody: In 2013, a Bollywood film sparked her curiosity about the mountains. What began with an NCC mountaineering camp in Manali led her into mountaineering, eventually to a career as a mountaineering instructor in Darjeeling, and later to Kashmir, where she first discovered skiing.
hero.profileBody2: In 2018, while training in alpine skiing in Kashmir, she came across the Norwegian legend Marit Bjørgen racing cross-country at the Winter Olympics. It was her first glimpse of the sport, and it stayed with her. Two years later she finally had the chance to try it herself, and what began as a chance to try something new became a passion. In 2021 she decided to pursue cross-country skiing full time.

profileFacts.v: Indian Himalayas · Europe · South America · New Zealand · Asia

hero.glanceHeadline: When the path doesn’t exist, you build one.
hero.glanceBody: From the coffee estates of Kodagu to international start lines, Bhavani Thekkada has forged a journey across continents, climates and seasons. In a sport with few pathways in India, she became the country’s first woman to win an international cross-country skiing medal. And she is still moving forward.

glanceSource.note: The first-woman claim is hers, supplied in her own homepage copy. Presented in her voice, attributed to her.

hero.profileBody3: Her father, Thekkada Nanjunda, has spent his life on the coffee farm. He never asked her to choose the conventional path. His advice was simple. If it makes you happy, do it.
hero.profileMission: Cross-country skiing still has little visibility in India. Bhavani wants to change that by making the sport easier to understand at home and creating a pathway others can follow.

journey.title: Kodagu to Davos
journey.lede: It begins in a district that has never had snow and ends on a World Cup start list at Davos.
journey.hinge: All the records, on the record
journey.hingeNote: Eleven starts, every one of them scored and published by FIS.

footprint.title: The map of six seasons
footprint.lede: One hundred and seven degrees of latitude separate her northernmost start from her southernmost. She races from inside the Arctic Circle to the far side of the Tropic of Capricorn.
footprint.mapNote: From 41°S at Antillanca to 66°N at Ruka. Kodagu sits almost exactly halfway between the two, at 12°N.

beyond.title: Two summits and four certificates
beyond.lede: Elbrus in 2018, the highest point in Europe. Ruapehu in 2019, an active volcano with a ski field on it, where she took the certification that let her teach abroad.

media.title: Press coverage
media.lede: Every article written about her, and six seasons of photographs, in one place.

ambition.title: The road to 2030
ambition.lede: Four seasons between here and a start list in the French Alps. Everything above this is on the record. What follows is a plan.

speaking.title: Athlete, speaker, storyteller
speaking.lede: Four talks, all of them drawn from the same decade of doing it. Each one takes a problem she actually had to solve and shows the working.

partners.title: Partnerships and support
partners.lede: She races a full FIS calendar largely at her own expense, and trains with other nations' squads because India fields none in her discipline. A season has a fixed shape, and support lands at particular points inside it.

beats.heading: Kodagu
beats.body: Born 14 May 1995 at Perur, near Napoklu, in the coffee-growing hills of Kodagu. It rains hard there for four months a year and it has never snowed. The nearest snow sits two thousand kilometres north and four thousand metres up.

beats.heading: The mountains came first
beats.body: She started mountaineering at nineteen, trained at ABVIMAS and at the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute in Darjeeling, and qualified as a mountaineer and instructor by 2017. There was no ski club to come up through. The mountains did that job.

beats.heading: The Republic Day contingent
beats.body: Selected for the NCC contingent at the Republic Day Parade in New Delhi, a year after the All India NCC camp.

beats.heading: Climbed Mount Elbrus
beats.body: She started alpine skiing. The same year she climbed Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 m the highest summit in Europe.

beats.heading: Certified abroad, then cross-country
beats.body: Took an international ski instructor certification in New Zealand, on an active volcano, then spent a season skiing abroad. Cross-country followed in 2020.

beats.heading: Onto the FIS circuit
beats.body: First FIS-scored races at Akureyri, northern Iceland, in January 2022. Planica followed in 2023 and Kazakhstan in 2024, then Harbin, Trondheim, Corralco and a first World Cup start at Ruka.

beyondFinishLine.lede: Qualifying is the target. It is not the whole of the ambition.

points.title: A sport with no home crowd
points.body: Every season she competes in is assembled from other countries' calendars. There is no home fixture for anyone to turn up to.

points.title: Explaining the sport
points.body: Most people in India have never watched a cross-country race. Part of the job is explaining what it is and why the distances are hard.

points.title: Athletes behind her
points.body: A pathway that exists on paper is different from one somebody has already walked. Being the first is the easy part to celebrate. Being followed is the harder one, and it is the one she is working on.

points.title: Proving the ceiling is higher
points.body: An Indian woman on a World Cup start list changes what the next selection meeting thinks is realistic.

beyondFinishLine.line: Cross-country has no home fixture in India and most people she meets have never watched a race. The longer project is to change that: make the sport legible at home, and turn a pathway that exists on paper into one somebody has already walked, so the next Indian woman on a start list is a selection, not a surprise.

speaking.lede: The storyteller is the reason she is here.

themes.title: Two thousand kilometres from snow
themes.body: How an athlete from a district with no winter reached a World Cup start list, and what the decade in between says about starting from wherever you actually are.

themes.title: Carrying the flag
themes.body: She led India into an Asian Winter Games as flagbearer. On being the first, being the only one, and what changes for the next woman on the team sheet.

themes.title: The mountain apprenticeship
themes.body: Before the racing there were glaciers, rope work and instructing jobs in Kashmir. What an unglamorous apprenticeship builds that talent alone does not.

themes.title: What endurance costs
themes.body: A 10 km race at a World Cup, planned to the heartbeat. The invisible work behind one visible hour, told honestly enough to be useful to any team.

speaking.availability: Her race season runs from late November to March. Dates inside it are limited.

skills.line: Most of the work happens before anyone is watching. She reached a World Cup start line from a place with no snow, and can show a room how to keep moving when nothing yet confirms it is working.
Endurance is a plan, not a feeling. A 10 km race is mapped to the heartbeat months before it is run, and she takes an audience inside how that hour is built and what it actually costs.

Being first is not the same as being ready. She carried India’s flag into an Asian Winter Games as the only one in her discipline, and speaks to what that asks of a person and what it opens for the next.
Talent takes more credit than it earns. Before the racing came glaciers, rope work and instructing jobs, and she makes the case for the unglamorous years that build somebody capable of the good ones.

Nobody funds what they cannot picture. Almost every season was paid for by explaining a sport the listener had never seen, and she can show how to make an unfamiliar idea land with the person who can back it.
A route only exists once somebody has walked it. She built one out of India in a sport that had none, and works on what it takes to make a path clear enough for the next person to follow.

invite.body: Bhavani speaks about building a career without a ready-made path, competing through uncertainty, and what years of disciplined work can make possible.

sport.context: Bhavani races both techniques across sprint and distance events.

headline.claim: The first Indian woman to win a medal in a FIS-scored cross-country race.
headline.line: Two bronzes in Chile in 2025, a World Cup start list at Ruka in the December that followed, and a sprint quarter-final at the Asian Winter Games. She reached all of it from a country with no cross-country course, no domestic race calendar and no coach in her discipline.
